(ch08-sec-hook)=
## The opening question

A campus wellness program runs an experiment. It recruits **200 students**,
randomly assigns **100 to a treatment group** (an 8-week activity-coaching
program) and **100 to a control group** (no coaching), and at the end records
each student's average daily *active minutes* from a wearable tracker. The
treatment group averaged more active minutes than the control group. The
program director is thrilled — until a skeptical colleague asks the only
question that matters:

> *"Random assignment splits people into two piles. Even if coaching did
> nothing at all, one pile will almost always come out a little ahead just by
> luck. How do you know your difference isn't just that luck?"*

That single question is the whole of this chapter. Let us put a number on it.

```{code-cell} r
:label: ch08-hook-compute

# Load the randomized two-group experiment (a *simulated* classroom dataset,
# committed with its generator; see the codebook). 200 students, 100 per arm.
fit <- read.csv("data/processed/fitness_tracker_sim.csv")

# Mean daily active minutes, "broken down BY group": that is what the mosaic
# formula active_minutes ~ group means -- read "~" as "by". It returns one mean
# per group, labeled with the group name.
grp_means <- mean(active_minutes ~ group, data = fit)
grp_means

# The observed difference: treatment mean minus control mean.
obs_diff <- unname(grp_means["treatment"] - grp_means["control"])
round(obs_diff, 3)
```

The treatment group averaged about **36.87** active minutes per day; the control
group about **27.94**. The observed difference is

$$
\bar{x}_{\text{treatment}} - \bar{x}_{\text{control}} \approx 36.87 - 27.94 = 8.92 \text{ minutes per day.}
$$

:::{note} Where this number comes from
Every statistic in this chapter is computed live from
`data/processed/fitness_tracker_sim.csv` (see its
[codebook](../../data/codebooks/fitness_tracker_sim.md)). This is a **simulated**
teaching dataset — a hypothetical randomized experiment with a built-in
coaching effect — labeled `_sim` and generated by a committed, seeded script
([CLAUDE.md §3.2](../about.md)). It is *not* a real study, and we never present
it as one. We use it because it has exactly the design — **random assignment to
two groups** — that the logic of hypothesis testing was invented to analyze.
:::

So the program *did* produce a 8.92-minute gap. The skeptic's question is whether
a gap that big could plausibly appear **even if coaching changes nothing**. By
the end of this chapter you will answer it with a number — and you will know
exactly what that number does, and does not, mean.

(ch08-sec-objectives)=
## Learning objectives

By the end of this chapter you will be able to:

1. **State** null and alternative hypotheses for a research question, and define
   the significance level $\alpha$, a Type I error, and a Type II error.
2. **Run** a randomization (permutation) test in R and use the simulated null
   distribution to find a p-value.
3. **Interpret** a p-value correctly, and connect a test decision to the
   corresponding confidence interval.
4. **Evaluate** the difference between *statistical* and *practical*
   significance, and the role sample size plays in each.
5. **Identify** the conditions a test requires and the consequences of violating
   them.

This chapter expands **ISRS sections 2.1–2.3** (randomization case studies and
hypothesis testing). It assumes you have met **sampling distributions and the
CLT** (Chapter 6) and **confidence intervals** (Chapter 7).

:::{note} The road map of every test (keep this nearby)

Every hypothesis test in this course — and in this chapter — walks the same six
steps, in the same order. Each section below fills in one of them:

1. **Hypotheses.** Write the null $H_0$ ("nothing is going on") and the
   alternative $H_A$ ("there's a real effect"). *(Section 1.)*
2. **Conditions.** Check that the method is allowed to be used here (e.g. random
   assignment, independence). *(Section 5.)*
3. **Test statistic.** Compute one number that measures how far the data sit from
   what $H_0$ expects — here, the difference in group means $D$. *(Section 2.)*
4. **p-value.** Find how often pure chance, with $H_0$ true, would produce a
   result at least this extreme. *(Sections 2–3.)*
5. **Decision.** Compare the p-value to a threshold $\alpha$: **reject $H_0$** or
   **fail to reject $H_0$**. *(Section 4.)*
6. **Confidence interval.** Report *how big* the effect plausibly is, not just
   whether it is there. *(Section 6.)*

If you ever feel lost in this chapter, come back here and find which step you are
on.
:::

---

(ch08-sec-hypotheses)=
## 1. Hypotheses: the two competing stories

### Intuition

Every hypothesis test is a contest between two stories about how the data were
produced.

- **The null story** is the boring one: *nothing is going on.* Coaching has no
  effect; any difference between the groups is just the luck of the random
  split. This is the **skeptic's position**, and — crucially — we *assume it is
  true* while we weigh the evidence, the way a court assumes a defendant
  innocent until the evidence says otherwise.
- **The alternative story** is the interesting one: *something is going on.*
  Coaching really does change active minutes, so the groups differ for a real
  reason, not just chance.

The test never tries to prove the alternative directly. Instead it asks: *if the
null story were true, how surprising would our data be?* If the data would be
very surprising under the null story, we abandon it in favor of the alternative.
If the data are unremarkable under the null story, we have no grounds to abandon
it. That asymmetry — we can reject the null but never *prove* it — is the
engine of the whole method.

### Formula (notation)

We write the two stories as the **null hypothesis** $H_0$ and the **alternative
hypothesis** $H_A$. For our two-group experiment they concern the difference in
**population** mean active minutes, $\mu_{\text{trt}} - \mu_{\text{ctrl}}$:

$$
H_0:\ \mu_{\text{trt}} - \mu_{\text{ctrl}} = 0
\qquad\qquad
H_A:\ \mu_{\text{trt}} - \mu_{\text{ctrl}} \neq 0
$$

Defining every symbol the first time it appears:

- $\mu_{\text{trt}}$ ("mu-treatment") — the **population** mean daily active
  minutes if *everyone* like our subjects received coaching. A fixed, unknown
  number (a *parameter*).
- $\mu_{\text{ctrl}}$ ("mu-control") — the population mean if no one received
  coaching.
- $H_0$ ("H-naught") — the **null hypothesis**: the two population means are
  equal, so their difference is $0$.
- $H_A$ ("H-A") — the **alternative hypothesis**: the means differ. The $\neq$
  makes this a **two-sided** alternative (we would care about a difference in
  *either* direction). If theory predicted a direction in advance we could use a
  **one-sided** alternative, $H_A:\ \mu_{\text{trt}} - \mu_{\text{ctrl}} > 0$.

Two rules that are easy to forget and costly to break:

1. Hypotheses are always about **parameters** — fixed, unknown population
   numbers like a population mean $\mu$ or a population proportion $p$ — never
   about **statistics**, the numbers we compute from a sample like a sample mean
   $\bar{x}$ ("x-bar") or a sample proportion $\hat{p}$ ("p-hat"). We already
   *know* $\bar{x}_{\text{trt}}
   - \bar{x}_{\text{ctrl}} = 8.92$; there is nothing to test about it. The
   question is what it tells us about the unknown $\mu$'s.
2. The hypotheses are chosen **before** looking at the data — or at least
   independently of the particular result we got — so we are not just drawing a
   target around wherever the arrow landed.

### In R

In this book we will *do* most of the testing by simulation (Section 2), but it
is worth seeing the group summaries that the hypotheses are about. In the mosaic
stack, `favstats()` gives a full teaching summary of a variable **broken down by
group** — again the `y ~ group` ("y by group") formula:

```{code-cell} r
:label: ch08-group-summaries

# favstats() summarizes active_minutes separately for each group: it prints
# min, Q1, median, Q3, max, the mean, the sd, the count n, and any missing.
favstats(active_minutes ~ group, data = fit)
```

Read the `mean`, `sd`, and `n` columns: $\bar{x}_{\text{trt}}$ and
$\bar{x}_{\text{ctrl}}$ are the two **sample means** (your best single-number
summary of each group), $s_{\text{trt}}$ and $s_{\text{ctrl}}$ are the two
**sample standard deviations** (how spread out each group is), and $n$ is the
number of students in each group. The treatment group
($\bar{x}_{\text{trt}} \approx 36.87$, $s_{\text{trt}} \approx 11.80$, $n = 100$)
sits above the control group ($\bar{x}_{\text{ctrl}} \approx 27.94$,
$s_{\text{ctrl}} \approx 13.02$, $n = 100$). $H_0$ says those two *population*
means are really equal; $H_A$ says they are not. Now we test.

---

(ch08-sec-randomization)=
## 2. The randomization test: chance, made visible

### Intuition

Here is the beautiful idea at the heart of this chapter. The students were
assigned to groups **by a coin flip we controlled.** So we can *re-run that coin
flip on a computer.*

If the null story is true — coaching does nothing — then each student's active
minutes were going to be whatever they were going to be, **regardless of which
group label they happened to get.** The labels "treatment" and "control" are, in
that world, just arbitrary stickers. So we can:

1. Pool all 200 active-minute values together.
2. **Shuffle** the 200 group labels and slap them back on at random — 100
   "treatment," 100 "control."
3. Recompute the difference in group means for this *fake* split.
4. Repeat thousands of times.

Each shuffle is a world in which the null story is literally true (we *know* the
labels are meaningless because we assigned them by shuffling). The thousands of
fake differences trace out the **null distribution**: the range of
group-mean differences that pure chance produces. Then we ask where our *real*
8.92-minute difference falls in that distribution. If it sits out in the far tail
— bigger than almost any difference chance alone produced — the null story
looks untenable.

### Formula (notation)

Let $D$ be the **test statistic**: the difference in sample means,

$$
D = \bar{x}_{\text{trt}} - \bar{x}_{\text{ctrl}}.
$$

We observed $D_{\text{obs}} \approx 8.92$. A **randomization** (or
**permutation**) **test** builds the null distribution of $D$ by repeatedly
shuffling the group labels. Let $D^{*}_1, D^{*}_2, \dots, D^{*}_{M}$ be the
differences from $M$ shuffles. The two-sided **p-value** is the fraction of
shuffles whose difference is at least as extreme as ours:

$$
\text{p-value} = \frac{\#\{\, i : |D^{*}_i| \ge |D_{\text{obs}}| \,\}}{M}.
$$

In words: *out of all the worlds where the null is true, what fraction produced
a difference as surprising as the one we actually saw?* A small p-value means
"almost none did," which is evidence against $H_0$.

- $D^{*}_i$ ("D-star-i") — the difference in means from the $i$-th label shuffle
  (a draw from the null distribution).
- $M$ — the number of shuffles (we use $M = 10{,}000$; more shuffles give a more
  precise p-value).
- $|D|$ — the absolute value of $D$; "at least as extreme" in a *two-sided* test
  means far from $0$ in **either** direction, so we compare absolute values.

### In R

We build the null distribution with base R's `replicate()` and `sample()`. This
is the transparent idiom every student should see at least once — you can read
the shuffle right off the page.

```{code-cell} r
:label: ch08-randomization-test

active <- fit$active_minutes
grp    <- fit$group
n_trt  <- sum(grp == "treatment")   # 100

# Observed test statistic D = xbar_trt - xbar_ctrl.
obs_diff <- mean(active[grp == "treatment"]) - mean(active[grp == "control"])

# Build the null distribution: shuffle the labels M times and recompute D.
# Each pass mirrors the four-step recipe above.
set.seed(2200)
M <- 10000
null_diffs <- replicate(M, {
  shuffled <- sample(grp)                       # step 2: shuffle the 200 labels
  mean(active[shuffled == "treatment"]) -       # steps 1 & 3: regroup and
    mean(active[shuffled == "control"])         #             recompute the gap
})

# Two-sided p-value: fraction of shuffles at least as extreme as observed.
p_value <- mean(abs(null_diffs) >= abs(obs_diff))
p_value
```

<!-- MATH-NOTE (non-blocking, verifier-flagged for awareness, not a failure):
     the exact analytic permutation SD of the active_minutes null distribution
     is 1.864 min (fresh simulations land ~1.86); the chapter's "about 1.88" is
     within simulation noise and does not affect the ~5-SD / p<0.0001 reading.
     Author may tighten "1.88" -> "1.86" for precision if desired. Copy-editor
     does not change the number. -->

The simulated null differences are centered near $0$ with a standard deviation
of about **1.86** minutes — that is the size of the wobble chance alone
produces. Our observed difference of **8.92** is almost **five** such wobbles
away from $0$. In **10,000** shuffles, **not one** reached a difference as
extreme as ours, so the estimated two-sided p-value is

$$
\text{p-value} = \frac{0}{10{,}000} < 0.0001 \quad\text{(dataset-derived, seed 2200).}
$$

:::{tip} Reading a p-value of "0"
A simulated p-value of $0/10{,}000$ does **not** mean the true probability is
exactly zero — it means it is *smaller than our simulation can resolve.* We
report it honestly as $p < 0.0001$ (i.e. $< 1/10{,}000$). If you need a more
precise tiny p-value, run more shuffles, or use the theory-based test in
Section 6, which gives $p \approx 8.8\times 10^{-7}$ for these data.
:::

Let us *see* the null distribution and where our result lands.

```r
null_df <- data.frame(diff = null_diffs)

ggplot(null_df, aes(x = diff)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = col_accent, colour = "white") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = obs_diff, colour = col_reject, linewidth = 1.1) +
  annotate("text", x = obs_diff, y = Inf, vjust = 1.5, hjust = 1.1,
           label = "observed\n8.92 min", colour = col_reject) +
  labs(
    title = "Where does our result fall under the null story?",
    subtitle = "10,000 shuffles of the group labels (coaching assumed to do nothing)",
    x = "Difference in mean active minutes (treatment - control)",
    y = "Number of shuffles"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

![Histogram of 10,000 simulated differences in group means under the null hypothesis, bell-shaped and centered at zero, spanning roughly negative five to positive five minutes. A tall vertical line at positive 8.92 minutes sits well to the right of every bar, indicating the observed difference is more extreme than any chance result.](data:image/png;base64,)

*Simulated null distribution of the difference in mean daily active minutes (treatment minus control) from 10,000 random shuffles of the group labels. The histogram is centered at zero with most values between about -5 and +5 minutes. A vertical line marks the observed difference of 8.92 minutes, which lies far to the right of the entire simulated distribution -- no shuffle produced a difference that large -- visually showing why the p-value is below 0.0001.*

The observed difference is off the right edge of everything chance produced.
The skeptic's "maybe it's just luck" story cannot account for a gap this big. We
**reject $H_0$**.

:::{important} Durable skill — Critical thinking: the logic of falsification
A randomization test is a machine for *falsification*. It never tries to confirm
that coaching works; it tries to **rule out the boring explanation** ("it was
just the random split") and only credits the interesting one when chance is left
with no plausible account of the data. This is exactly how a careful analyst —
or a careful juror, auditor, or engineer — reasons on the job: **state the
mundane explanation first, then see whether the evidence can survive it.** When
a dashboard at work shows that version B of a web page "beat" version A, the
durable habit this chapter builds is to ask, before celebrating, *"how big a gap
would I expect from random noise alone?"* — and to know how to compute it.
:::

---

(ch08-sec-pvalue)=
## 3. The p-value: what it is, and what it is not

### Intuition

The p-value is the single most misread number in statistics, so we will be very
careful. It answers one specific question:

> **If the null hypothesis were true, what is the probability of getting a result
> at least as extreme as the one we actually observed?**

Small p-value $\Rightarrow$ our data would be *surprising* in a world where
$H_0$ is true $\Rightarrow$ evidence *against* $H_0$. Large p-value
$\Rightarrow$ our data are *unremarkable* under $H_0$ $\Rightarrow$ no evidence
against it.

The direction of the conditional is everything. The p-value is the probability
of *the data*, computed *assuming the null*. It is **not** the probability that
the null is true.

### Formula (notation)

$$
\text{p-value} = P\big(\text{statistic at least as extreme as observed} \;\big|\; H_0 \text{ true}\big).
$$

The vertical bar "$\mid$" reads "given." Read left to right: the probability of
an extreme statistic, *given* $H_0$. Reversing it — "the probability $H_0$ is
true given the data" — is a different quantity entirely, and the test does not
compute it.

:::{warning} Four ways people misread a p-value (and the truth)

| The misreading | Why it's wrong |
|---|---|
| "p = 0.03 means there's a 3% chance $H_0$ is true." | The p-value assumes $H_0$ is true; it cannot also be the chance $H_0$ is true. |
| "p = 0.30 proves $H_0$ is true (no effect)." | Failing to reject is *not* proof of $H_0$ — maybe the effect is real but small, or $n$ is too small to detect it. |
| "A smaller p-value means a bigger effect." | The p-value mixes effect size **and** sample size. A tiny effect with huge $n$ can give a microscopic p-value. |
| "p = 0.049 and p = 0.051 are worlds apart." | They are essentially identical evidence; the $0.05$ line is a convention, not a law of nature. |
:::

### In R

Our randomization p-value was $< 0.0001$. We can summarize the evidence
compactly:

```{code-cell} r
:label: ch08-pvalue-summary

cat("Observed difference D_obs :", round(obs_diff, 3), "minutes\n")
cat("Shuffles M                :", M, "\n")
cat("Shuffles >= |D_obs|       :", sum(abs(null_diffs) >= abs(obs_diff)), "\n")
cat("Two-sided p-value         :", format(p_value), " (report as < 1e-04)\n")
```

---

(ch08-sec-errors)=
## 4. Decisions, $\alpha$, and the two ways to be wrong

### Intuition

A test ends in a decision: **reject $H_0$** or **fail to reject $H_0$.** In plain
words, **"reject $H_0$"** means *the data are surprising enough that we stop
believing the boring "nothing is going on" story*; **"fail to reject $H_0$"**
means *the data are not surprising enough to abandon that story — so we keep it,
for now.* (Never "accept $H_0$" — we only ever fail to find enough evidence
against it; that is a real difference, not word-play, and Q1 of the FAQ explains
why.) To decide, we pick a threshold *in advance* called the **significance
level**, written $\alpha$ ("alpha"). $\alpha$ is just *how surprising the data
must be before we are willing to reject* $H_0$. The usual choice is
$\alpha = 0.05$. The rule is simple:

$$
\text{if } \text{p-value} < \alpha \ \Rightarrow\ \text{reject } H_0;
\qquad
\text{if } \text{p-value} \ge \alpha \ \Rightarrow\ \text{fail to reject } H_0.
$$

Because we are deciding under uncertainty, we can be wrong in two ways. Picture a
smoke alarm:

- A **Type I error** is a *false alarm*: the alarm shrieks but there is no fire.
  In testing, that is **rejecting $H_0$ when $H_0$ is actually true** — declaring
  an effect that isn't real.
- A **Type II error** is a *missed fire*: the house is burning and the alarm
  stays silent. That is **failing to reject $H_0$ when $H_A$ is actually true** —
  missing a real effect.

### Formula (notation)

$$
\alpha = P(\text{Type I error}) = P(\text{reject } H_0 \mid H_0 \text{ true}),
\qquad
\beta = P(\text{Type II error}) = P(\text{fail to reject } H_0 \mid H_A \text{ true}).
$$

- $\alpha$ — the significance level, *and* the long-run probability of a Type I
  error. By choosing $\alpha = 0.05$ you accept a 5% false-alarm rate when the
  null is true.
- $\beta$ ("beta") — the probability of a Type II error.
- **Power** $= 1 - \beta$ — the probability of *correctly* detecting a real
  effect. Bigger samples and bigger true effects raise power.

The two errors trade off. Lowering $\alpha$ (say to $0.01$) makes false alarms
rarer but missed fires more common (larger $\beta$). You cannot drive both to
zero at once; you choose the balance that fits the stakes.

|  | $H_0$ is **true** | $H_0$ is **false** |
|---|---|---|
| **Reject $H_0$** | Type I error ($\alpha$) | Correct (power $= 1-\beta$) |
| **Fail to reject $H_0$** | Correct | Type II error ($\beta$) |

### In R

Here is $\alpha$ made tangible. We *simulate a world where $H_0$ is exactly
true* — random labels on numbers that share one common distribution — and check
how often a 5%-level test cries "effect!" anyway. It should be about 5%.

```{code-cell} r
:label: ch08-type-1-sim

set.seed(2200)
# A population where the null is TRUE: everyone is drawn from the SAME distribution.
type1_flags <- replicate(2000, {
  y  <- rnorm(200, mean = 30, sd = 12)             # no real group difference
  g  <- sample(rep(c("trt", "ctrl"), each = 100))  # random labels
  p  <- t.test(y ~ g)$p.value                       # quick theory-based test
  p < 0.05                                          # did we (wrongly) reject?
})
mean(type1_flags)   # empirical Type I error rate ~ 0.05
```

The false-alarm rate comes out near **0.05**, exactly as $\alpha$ promises: when
the null is true, a 5%-level test still rejects about one time in twenty. That is
the *price* of the method, fixed in advance — and the reason a single
"significant" result is never the end of the story.

---

(ch08-sec-significance)=
## 5. Significance vs. importance, and the conditions

### Intuition

A result can be **statistically significant** (small p-value: unlikely to be
chance) yet **practically trivial** (the effect is too small to matter). The two
are different questions, and you need both:

- *Statistical* significance asks: **is the effect real, or just noise?** (the
  p-value).
- *Practical* significance asks: **is the effect big enough to care about?** (the
  effect size and its confidence interval).

The villain that lets them diverge is **sample size**. With a large enough $n$,
*any* nonzero difference — however tiny — eventually becomes statistically
significant, because the standard error shrinks toward zero. So "significant"
on a huge dataset can mean "real but minuscule," and "not significant" on a tiny
dataset can mean "we couldn't tell." Always report the **effect size** alongside
the p-value.

Tests also rest on **conditions**. For the randomization test the key one is
that the grouping was, in the null world, **exchangeable** — most cleanly
guaranteed by *random assignment* (which our experiment has). For the
theory-based two-sample test (Section 6) the conditions are **independence**
(within and between groups) and **approximate normality** of each group's
distribution (automatically satisfied for the means when each $n \ge 30$, by the
CLT of Chapter 6). Violating independence is the most damaging: it invalidates
the standard error, and a test with the wrong standard error gives the wrong
p-value.

### Formula (notation): a simple effect size

One common effect size for a difference of means is **Cohen's $d$**, the
difference expressed in pooled-standard-deviation units:

$$
d = \frac{\bar{x}_{\text{trt}} - \bar{x}_{\text{ctrl}}}{s_p},
\qquad
s_p = \sqrt{\frac{(n_1-1)s_1^2 + (n_2-1)s_2^2}{n_1+n_2-2}}.
$$

- $s_p$ — the **pooled standard deviation**, a weighted blend of the two group
  SDs ($s_1, s_2$) using their sample sizes ($n_1, n_2$). Think of it as a
  class-size-weighted average of the two spreads: the bigger group's SD, being
  estimated from more data, counts for more.
- $d$ — how many standard deviations apart the group means are. Rough field
  conventions: $|d|\approx 0.2$ small, $0.5$ medium, $0.8$ large.

### In R

```{code-cell} r
:label: ch08-effect-size

x1 <- active[grp == "treatment"]; x2 <- active[grp == "control"]
n1 <- length(x1); n2 <- length(x2)
sp <- sqrt(((n1 - 1) * var(x1) + (n2 - 1) * var(x2)) / (n1 + n2 - 2))
cohens_d <- (mean(x1) - mean(x2)) / sp
round(cohens_d, 3)
```

Cohen's $d \approx 0.72$ — close to a **large** effect. So our coaching result is
both *statistically* significant ($p < 0.0001$) **and** *practically*
meaningful (a near-large effect of about 8.9 extra active minutes a day). That is
the conclusion you want to be able to defend: not just "significant," but
"significant **and** sizable."

:::{important} Durable skill — Quantitative reasoning: never report a p-value alone
On the job, "the difference is statistically significant" is an incomplete — and
sometimes misleading — sentence. A retailer with ten million transactions can
find that a checkout tweak "significantly" raises spending by four cents; a
clinic with twelve patients might miss a life-changing drug effect for lack of
power. The durable reasoning skill is to **always pair the p-value with an
effect size and a confidence interval**, and to read sample size as the hidden
dial behind both. "Is it real?" and "is it big enough to act on?" are two
questions, and a competent analyst answers both.
:::

---

(ch08-sec-ci-connection)=
## 6. Connecting the test to a confidence interval

### Intuition

A hypothesis test and a confidence interval are two views of the same evidence.
A **95% confidence interval** for the difference in means is the set of
difference-values that a two-sided test at $\alpha = 0.05$ would *not* reject. So
there is a clean equivalence:

> **The 95% CI for the difference excludes $0$** $\iff$ **the two-sided test
> rejects $H_0:\ \text{difference} = 0$ at $\alpha = 0.05$.**

If $0$ is a plausible value for the difference (inside the interval), you cannot
rule out "no effect." If $0$ is *not* plausible (outside the interval), you
reject "no effect" — and the interval additionally tells you *how big* the
effect plausibly is, which the p-value alone never does.

### Formula (notation)

The theory-based (Welch) two-sample $t$ interval and test use

$$
t = \frac{(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) - 0}{SE}, \qquad
SE = \sqrt{\frac{s_1^2}{n_1} + \frac{s_2^2}{n_2}}, \qquad
(\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2) \pm t^{*}\, SE,
$$

where $SE$ is the **standard error** of the difference, $t^{*}$ is the critical
value from the $t$-distribution (Chapter 10 develops this fully), and the
$\pm t^{*}SE$ piece is the **margin of error**. We let mosaic's `t.test()` do the
arithmetic; its printout puts the test (the $t$ statistic and p-value) and the
confidence interval for the difference side by side.

### In R

```{code-cell} r
:label: ch08-infer-two-means

# Theory-based companion to the randomization test: the Welch two-sample t-test,
# via the mosaic formula active_minutes ~ group.
#
# t.test reports the difference as (first factor level) - (second factor level).
# R orders factor levels alphabetically by default, which would put "control"
# first and report control - treatment (a negative difference). To keep every
# number in this chapter in the intuitive *treatment minus control* direction --
# matching the 8.92-minute gap and the randomization test above -- we make
# "treatment" the first level once, here, and reuse it for the sleep example.
fit$group <- factor(fit$group, levels = c("treatment", "control"))

# t.test prints the test (t, df, p-value), the 95% confidence interval for the
# difference, and each group's mean. With "treatment" as the first level, the
# CI reads treatment - control (positive), exactly as the prose describes.
res <- t.test(active_minutes ~ group, data = fit)
res
```

The `Welch Two Sample t-test` block reports $t \approx 5.08$ (df $\approx 196$),
a p-value of about $8.8\times10^{-7}$, a **95% confidence interval for the
difference of about $(5.46,\ 12.39)$ minutes**, and the two group means
(`mean in group treatment` $\approx 36.87$, `mean in group control`
$\approx 27.94$). The interval lies **entirely above $0$**, so the test rejects
$H_0$: the two views agree, as they must. And notice what the interval adds: not
merely "the effect is real," but "the extra active minutes plausibly run from
about 5.5 to 12.4 a day."

```{code-cell} r
:label: ch08-ci-values

cat("Welch t            :", round(res$statistic, 3), "\n")
cat("p-value            :", format(res$p.value), "\n")
cat("95% CI for diff    : (", round(res$conf.int[1], 3), ",",
    round(res$conf.int[2], 3), ")\n")
cat("CI excludes 0?     :", (res$conf.int[1] > 0 | res$conf.int[2] < 0), "\n")
```

The randomization p-value ($<0.0001$) and the theory-based p-value
($\approx 8.8\times10^{-7}$) tell the same story for these data — strong evidence
against $H_0$ — which is reassuring: when conditions hold, the simulation and the
formula agree.

:::{tip} Going deeper (optional) — why the CI/test equivalence is *exact*, and the one-sided wrinkle
:class: dropdown

Skip this box if you are still settling the basics; it is enrichment, not a
required skill.

The equivalence "95% CI excludes $0$ $\iff$ two-sided test rejects at
$\alpha=0.05$" is not a coincidence — it is built from the *same* standard error
and critical value. The two-sided test rejects when

$$
\left|\frac{(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)-0}{SE}\right| > t^{*},
\quad\text{i.e. when}\quad
\big|(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)\big| > t^{*}\,SE .
$$

The 95% interval is exactly $(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2) \pm t^{*}SE$. So "$0$ falls
outside the interval" and "the test statistic exceeds $t^{*}$" are *algebraically
the same inequality* — same $SE$, same $t^{*}$. That is why they can never
disagree for a two-sided test at the matching level.

**The one-sided wrinkle.** This clean equivalence is for a *two-sided* test
matched with a *two-sided* (ordinary) interval. A one-sided test at $\alpha$
pairs with a *one-sided* confidence bound, not the usual two-sided interval — so
do not check a one-sided test against a two-sided interval and expect them to
line up. And note the duality has limits: the **theory-based** CI matches the
**theory-based** $t$-test exactly, but the **randomization** p-value and the
$t$-interval are different machines that merely *agree closely* when conditions
hold, as they do here. When you need them to correspond perfectly, match like
with like.
:::

---

(ch08-sec-worked)=
## Worked examples

Each example follows the same arc: **intuition $\rightarrow$ formula $\rightarrow$ computation $\rightarrow$
interpretation.** At least one uses the Kern-relevant classroom dataset.

(ch08-sec-ex1)=
### Example 1 — A borderline result: does coaching change sleep?

**(Dataset: `fitness_tracker_sim`, variable `sleep_hours`.)**

*Intuition.* The same experiment also recorded average nightly sleep. Coaching
*might* improve sleep, but if it does the effect looks small. This is the
interesting case where the answer is "barely." We test
$H_0:\ \mu_{\text{trt}} - \mu_{\text{ctrl}} = 0$ against the two-sided
$H_A:\ \mu_{\text{trt}} - \mu_{\text{ctrl}} \neq 0$ for sleep hours.

*Formula.* Same randomization machinery as Section 2, with $D =
\bar{x}_{\text{trt}} - \bar{x}_{\text{ctrl}}$ for `sleep_hours`, and the
two-sided p-value $\#\{|D^*_i| \ge |D_{\text{obs}}|\}/M$.

*Computation.*

```{code-cell} r
:label: ch08-ex1-sleep

sleep <- fit$sleep_hours
obs_sleep <- mean(sleep[grp == "treatment"]) - mean(sleep[grp == "control"])

set.seed(2200)
null_sleep <- replicate(10000, {
  s <- sample(grp)
  mean(sleep[s == "treatment"]) - mean(sleep[s == "control"])
})
p_sleep <- mean(abs(null_sleep) >= abs(obs_sleep))

cat("Observed difference :", round(obs_sleep, 3), "hours\n")
cat("Randomization p     :", round(p_sleep, 4), "\n")

# Theory-based companion (Welch t) for the matching confidence interval.
# fit$group still has "treatment" as its first level (set in Section 6),
# so this difference and CI also read treatment - control (positive).
res_sleep <- t.test(sleep_hours ~ group, data = fit)
res_sleep
```

*Interpretation.* The observed difference is about **0.273 hours** (≈ 16 minutes)
more sleep in the treatment group. The randomization p-value is about
**0.043**, and the Welch test gives $p \approx 0.048$ with a **95% CI of about
$(0.003,\ 0.542)$ hours.** Both p-values are *just under* $0.05$, and the CI's
lower end ($0.003$) sits *just above* $0$ — the test rejects $H_0$, but only
barely, and the effect could be as small as a couple of minutes a night. This is
the textbook "statistically significant but practically marginal" verdict: a
real-but-tiny effect that a careful analyst would flag as **not robust** and
**too small to be sure it matters**, the opposite of the decisive active-minutes
result.
A different random seed could nudge the p-value to either side of $0.05$ —
which is precisely why the $0.05$ line is a convention, not a cliff.

(ch08-sec-ex2)=
### Example 2 — A one-sided test on resting heart rate

**(Dataset: `fitness_tracker_sim`, variable `resting_hr`.)**

*Intuition.* Physiologically, more activity should *lower* resting heart rate, so
here a **directional** prediction is justified in advance. We test
$H_0:\ \mu_{\text{trt}} - \mu_{\text{ctrl}} = 0$ against the one-sided
$H_A:\ \mu_{\text{trt}} - \mu_{\text{ctrl}} < 0$ (treatment lower).

*Formula.* For a one-sided "less" alternative, the p-value counts only shuffles
at least as **low** as the observed difference:
$\text{p-value} = \#\{D^*_i \le D_{\text{obs}}\}/M$.

*Computation.*

```{code-cell} r
:label: ch08-ex2-hr

hr <- fit$resting_hr
obs_hr <- mean(hr[grp == "treatment"]) - mean(hr[grp == "control"])

set.seed(2200)
null_hr <- replicate(10000, {
  s <- sample(grp)
  mean(hr[s == "treatment"]) - mean(hr[s == "control"])
})
p_hr_one_sided <- mean(null_hr <= obs_hr)   # one-sided "less"

cat("Observed difference :", round(obs_hr, 3), "bpm\n")
cat("One-sided p (<)     :", round(p_hr_one_sided, 4), "\n")
```

*Interpretation.* The treatment group's resting heart rate is about **3.29 bpm
lower**, and the one-sided randomization p-value is about **0.0008** — far below
$0.05$. We reject $H_0$ in favor of "coaching lowers resting heart rate." Because
the direction was predicted *before* seeing the data (on physiological grounds),
the one-sided test is legitimate here. **Warning:** choosing one-sided *after*
peeking at which direction the data went is a form of cheating that secretly
doubles your false-alarm rate. Decide the direction first, or stay two-sided.

(ch08-sec-ex3)=
### Example 3 — Reading a published claim (no new data)

*Intuition.* A press release says: *"In a randomized trial of 40,000 shoppers, a
new app layout raised average order value by \$0.06 (p = 0.001)."* Should the
company rebuild its app?

*Formula.* The reasoning is the significance-vs-importance logic of Section 5.
With $n = 40{,}000$ the standard error $SE = s/\sqrt{n}$ is tiny, so even a
$\$0.06$ difference yields a large test statistic and a microscopic p-value.

*Computation (a back-of-envelope illustration).* Suppose order values have
$s \approx \$8$. Then for the difference, $SE \approx 8\sqrt{1/20000 + 1/20000}
\approx \$0.08$, giving $t \approx 0.06/0.08 \approx 0.75$ — actually *not*
significant at that $s$. The point: the verdict hinges entirely on $s$ and $n$,
not on whether \$0.06 matters to a customer.

*Interpretation.* "p = 0.001" tells you the six-cent difference is probably
**real**; it tells you nothing about whether six cents is **worth a redesign.**
The right follow-up questions are the *effect size* (\$0.06 — trivial per order,
but times 40,000 orders?) and the *confidence interval* for the lift. A
statistically significant result on a giant sample is an invitation to ask "how
big, and big enough for what?", never a finished argument. (This example uses no
curated dataset; the dollar figures are an illustrative scenario, not data.)

(ch08-sec-ex4)=
### Example 4 — Steps: confirming with two methods

**(Dataset: `fitness_tracker_sim`, variable `steps`.)**

*Intuition.* Daily step count is the headline fitness measure. We expect coaching
to raise it; test two-sided to stay honest, and confirm that the randomization
test and the theory-based test agree.

*Formula.* Randomization p-value (two-sided) as in Section 2, plus the Welch
$t = (\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2)/SE$ companion.

*Computation.*

```{code-cell} r
:label: ch08-ex4-steps

steps <- fit$steps
obs_steps <- mean(steps[grp == "treatment"]) - mean(steps[grp == "control"])

set.seed(2200)
null_steps <- replicate(10000, {
  s <- sample(grp)
  mean(steps[s == "treatment"]) - mean(steps[s == "control"])
})
p_steps <- mean(abs(null_steps) >= abs(obs_steps))

cat("Observed difference :", round(obs_steps, 1), "steps/day\n")
cat("Randomization p     :", round(p_steps, 4), "\n")

res_steps <- t.test(steps ~ group, data = fit)
res_steps
```

*Interpretation.* The treatment group walked about **942 more steps per day.**
The randomization p-value is about **0.0018** and the Welch test gives
$p \approx 0.0021$ — the two methods agree closely, both well below $0.05$. We
reject $H_0$: coaching raised step count. With a difference near 942 steps
(roughly a 13% lift over the control mean of about 7,171), this is a result that
is *both* statistically significant *and* practically meaningful — the kind of
clean win the active-minutes result also gave us, and a useful contrast with the
borderline sleep result of Example 1.

(ch08-sec-tryit)=
## Try it yourself

The single most important idea of this chapter is that **a p-value is just the
tail proportion of the null distribution.** The interactive figure below lets you
*see* that. The blue histogram is a randomization null distribution built exactly
as in Section 2 — thousands of shuffled-label differences, all from a world where
the null is true. **Drag the slider** to set a hypothetical observed test
statistic $|D|$; the figure shades the two-sided tail beyond $\pm|D|$ and reports
the simulated p-value as the share of shuffles in that shaded tail. Slide right
and watch both the shaded area and the p-value shrink — and notice where the tail
proportion crosses $0.05$.

:::{figure} #fig-null-pvalue-sim
:label: ch08-fig-null-pvalue-interactive
:alt: Interactive histogram of a randomization null distribution of differences in group means, bell-shaped and centered on a green dotted no-effect line at zero, spanning about negative six to positive six. A slider sets an observed test statistic; the two-sided tail beyond plus and minus the observed value is shaded in hatched vermillion between two dashed boundary lines, and a boxed annotation reports the simulated p-value as the proportion of shuffles falling in that shaded tail. As the slider moves the observed statistic outward, the shaded tail and the reported p-value both shrink, dropping below 0.05 around an observed value of four.
**The p-value is the tail of the null distribution (simulated).** — Drag the slider to set the observed statistic; the shaded two-sided tail is the simulated p-value.
:::

Reinforce this chapter with the matching interactive tools:

  Launch with `shiny::runApp("shiny-explorer")` from the repo root and open the
  **One/Two-Sample Tests** tab.
- **Jupyter Lab 8 — `labs/lab08-hypothesis-testing.ipynb`** (R kernel). The lab
  walks you through building a null distribution by hand, computing a p-value,

  `fitness_tracker_sim` data loads with
  `read.csv("data/processed/fitness_tracker_sim.csv")`.

(ch08-sec-summary)=
## Chapter summary

- A **hypothesis test** weighs two stories: the **null** $H_0$ ("nothing is going
  on," assumed true while we judge) and the **alternative** $H_A$ ("there's a
  real effect"). Hypotheses are about **parameters**, set **before** seeing the
  result.
- A **randomization (permutation) test** builds the **null distribution** by
  repeatedly **shuffling the group labels**, then asks where the observed
  statistic falls. The **p-value** is the fraction of shuffles at least as
  extreme as our result.
- The **p-value** is $P(\text{data this extreme}\mid H_0)$ — *not* the
  probability $H_0$ is true, *not* an effect size. Small p-value $\Rightarrow$
  evidence against $H_0$.
- Decide by comparing the p-value to the **significance level** $\alpha$ (often
  $0.05$). A **Type I error** is a false alarm (rate $\alpha$); a **Type II
  error** is a missed effect (rate $\beta$); **power** $= 1-\beta$.
- **Statistical** significance ("is it real?") and **practical** significance
  ("is it big enough?") are different questions; **sample size** drives both.
  Always report an **effect size** and **confidence interval** with the p-value.
- A **95% CI excluding $0$** is equivalent to a **two-sided test rejecting at
  $\alpha = 0.05$** — and the CI additionally says *how big* the effect plausibly
  is.

---

(ch08-sec-faq)=
## FAQ

**Q1. Why can't I ever "accept" or "prove" the null hypothesis?**
Because failing to find evidence against $H_0$ is not the same as evidence *for*
it. A large p-value can mean "no effect," but it can equally mean "there is an
effect, but my sample was too small to detect it." Absence of evidence is not
evidence of absence, so we say "fail to reject," never "accept."

**Q2. What's the difference between a randomization test and the $t$-test?**
They answer the same question by different routes. The **randomization test**
*simulates* the null distribution by shuffling labels — it needs almost no
assumptions when you have random assignment, and you can literally see it work.
The **$t$-test** uses a mathematical formula for the null distribution that
relies on conditions (independence, approximate normality). When conditions hold,
they agree closely, as Examples 4 and the main text show.

**Q3. Is $\alpha = 0.05$ a law? Can I use a different threshold?**
$0.05$ is a *convention*, not a law. You choose $\alpha$ in advance to match the
stakes: a smaller $\alpha$ (e.g. $0.01$) when a false alarm is costly, a larger
one when missing a real effect is worse. What you must *not* do is pick $\alpha$
*after* seeing the p-value to get the verdict you wanted.

**Q4. When is a one-sided test okay?**
Only when you can justify the direction **before** looking at the data — from
theory, prior research, or the logic of the problem (as with resting heart rate
in Example 2). Choosing one-sided after seeing which way the data leaned secretly
doubles your false-alarm rate and is not legitimate.

**Q5. My p-value came out as 0. Is the effect *impossible* under the null?**
No. A simulated p-value of $0/10{,}000$ means "smaller than this simulation can
resolve," i.e. $< 0.0001$. Report it that way. Run more shuffles, or use the
theory-based test, for a more precise tiny value.

**Q6. The result is "significant" — does that mean it's important?**
Not necessarily. Statistical significance says the effect is probably real, not
that it is large or useful. Check the **effect size** (e.g. Cohen's $d$) and the
**confidence interval**. With a big sample, even a trivial difference can be
significant.

**Q7. Why do we compare *absolute* values for a two-sided p-value?**
Because a two-sided alternative ($\neq$) treats a difference as "extreme" if it
is far from $0$ in **either** direction. Comparing $|D^*_i| \ge |D_{\text{obs}}|$
counts shuffles that are extreme on the left *or* the right. A one-sided test
counts only one tail.

**Q8. What breaks the test if I ignore the conditions?**
Independence is the big one. If observations are not independent (e.g. repeated
measures treated as separate subjects), the true standard error is wrong, so the
p-value is wrong — usually too small, giving false alarms. Random assignment
protects the randomization test; random sampling and independence protect the
theory-based test.

---

(ch08-sec-practice)=
## Practice problems

Problems are auto-numbered. **Odd-numbered** problems have short answers in the
[answer appendix](../appendix/answers.md); full worked solutions for every
problem live in the instructor key. Unless stated otherwise, use
$\alpha = 0.05$ and the `fitness_tracker_sim` dataset
(`fit <- read.csv("data/processed/fitness_tracker_sim.csv")`).

:::{note}

1. State, in words and in symbols, the null and alternative hypotheses for a
   two-sided test of whether coaching changes mean daily active minutes.

2. A study reports $\bar{x}_{\text{trt}} - \bar{x}_{\text{ctrl}} = 12$ and a
   two-sided randomization p-value of $0.30$. In one sentence, what do you
   conclude, and what do you *not* conclude?

3. Explain why hypotheses are written about $\mu$ (a parameter) and never about
   $\bar{x}$ (a statistic).

4. In a randomization test, what exactly are you shuffling, and what null-world
   assumption makes the shuffle valid?

5. Define a Type I error and a Type II error in the context of the coaching
   experiment (use the words "coaching" and "active minutes").

6. A test gives $p = 0.5$. Sketch in words where the observed statistic sits in
   the null distribution.

7. True or false, and explain: "A p-value of $0.02$ means there is a 2% chance
   the null hypothesis is true."

8. Why might a real effect produce a *large* (non-significant) p-value? Name the
   most common reason.

9. Using the chapter's `active_minutes` randomization output, the observed
   difference (8.92) was about how many null-distribution standard deviations
   (≈ 1.86) away from $0$? Show the arithmetic.

10. Explain the equivalence between a 95% confidence interval that excludes $0$
    and a two-sided test that rejects $H_0$ at $\alpha = 0.05$.

11. For the `sleep_hours` example, the randomization p-value was about $0.043$
    and the 95% CI was about $(0.003, 0.542)$ hours. Are these two results
    consistent? Explain why.

12. You run a one-sided test ("greater") and get a two-sided-style p-value of
    $0.08$ from your code. If the data went in the predicted direction, what is
    the one-sided p-value, and is it significant at $0.05$?

13. Write the R code (base R) to build a null distribution of the difference in
    mean `resting_hr` between groups using 5,000 shuffles, and to compute a
    two-sided p-value.

14. A colleague lowers $\alpha$ from $0.05$ to $0.01$. What happens to the Type I
    error rate, and what happens to the Type II error rate (qualitatively)?

15. Cohen's $d$ for active minutes was about $0.72$. Interpret this number for a
    non-statistician in one or two sentences.

16. Explain why running 50 separate hypothesis tests at $\alpha = 0.05$ on data
    with *no* real effects will, on average, still produce about 2–3
    "significant" results. (This previews the multiple-comparisons issue of
    Chapters 11–12.)

17. Run the `active_minutes` randomization test with a *different* seed (e.g.
    `set.seed(7)`). Does your p-value change a lot? Why or why not?

18. A study with $n = 1{,}000{,}000$ finds a "highly significant" ($p < 0.0001$)
    difference of $0.01$ units between two groups. Write the two questions a
    careful analyst should ask before acting on this.

19. For the `steps` variable, state $H_0$ and $H_A$ for a two-sided test, then
    report (from the chapter) the observed difference and the randomization
    p-value, and give your decision at $\alpha = 0.05$.

20. Explain, in plain language a manager could follow, the difference between
    "statistically significant" and "practically important."

21. Suppose a randomization test gives $p = 0.049$ and a second, near-identical
    study gives $p = 0.051$. How different is the *evidence* in the two studies?
    What does this say about treating $0.05$ as a hard cutoff?

22. The chapter's Type I error simulation rejected the (true) null about 5% of
    the time. Explain how this number is the *definition* of $\alpha$ made
    visible.

23. Using `t.test(active_minutes ~ group, data = fit)`, which pieces of the
    printed output tell you (a) the decision and (b) the size of the effect?
    Name them.

24. Why does a two-sided test compare $|D^*| \ge |D_{\text{obs}}|$ while a
    one-sided "greater" test compares $D^* \ge D_{\text{obs}}$? Draw the
    connection to the shape of $H_A$.

25. A researcher checks their data, sees the treatment mean is higher, and
    *then* decides to run a one-sided "greater" test to get a smaller p-value.
    Explain why this inflates the false-alarm rate and what they should have done
    instead.

:::

---

:::{tip} A note on reproducibility
:class: dropdown
Every numeric result in this chapter is computed from
`data/processed/fitness_tracker_sim.csv` with the chapter seed `set.seed(2200)`.
Re-running the chapter reproduces every figure and p-value exactly. The
randomization p-values are *simulation estimates*; with $M = 10{,}000$ shuffles
they are precise to roughly $\pm 0.01$, which is why the borderline `sleep_hours`
result (p ≈ 0.043–0.048) should be read as "right around $0.05$," not as a
sharp verdict.
:::

## Resumen en español

:::{note} Resumen del capítulo
:class: dropdown

En este capítulo aprendiste la lógica central de la prueba de hipótesis
(hypothesis test): un método para decidir si la diferencia que observaste en tus
datos pudo haber ocurrido simplemente por azar, o si refleja un efecto real.

El punto de partida es plantear dos historias en competencia. La hipótesis nula
(null hypothesis), $H_0$, dice que no está pasando nada — cualquier diferencia
entre grupos se debe a la suerte del sorteo. La hipótesis alternativa (alternative
hypothesis), $H_A$, dice que sí existe un efecto real. Las hipótesis se escriben
siempre en términos de parámetros (parameters) — números fijos de la población,
como la media poblacional (population mean) $\mu$ — nunca sobre estadísticos de
la muestra como $\bar{x}$.

Para poner esta idea a prueba usamos una prueba de aleatorización (randomization
test): tomamos las 200 observaciones del experimento de coaching del capítulo,
mezclamos las etiquetas de grupo al azar miles de veces, y recalculamos la
diferencia de medias en cada mezcla. Esas miles de diferencias forman la
distribución nula (null distribution) — la variación que el azar solo puede
producir. Luego preguntamos: ¿qué fracción de esas mezclas generó una diferencia
tan grande como la que observamos? Esa fracción es el valor p (p-value).

En el ejemplo principal, la diferencia observada en minutos activos diarios fue de
aproximadamente 8.92 minutos, y ninguna de las 10,000 mezclas la igualó, así que
el valor p fue menor que 0.0001. Cuando el valor p es menor que el nivel de
significancia (significance level) $\alpha$ — que convencionalmente se fija en
0.05 — rechazamos $H_0$.

Al decidir, puedes equivocarte de dos formas: un error Tipo I (Type I error) es
rechazar $H_0$ cuando en realidad es verdadera (una falsa alarma cuya tasa es
exactamente $\alpha$); un error Tipo II (Type II error) es no rechazar $H_0$
cuando la alternativa es verdadera (perder un efecto real). La potencia (power)
de la prueba es $1 - \beta$, la probabilidad de detectar un efecto que existe.

Un hallazgo estadísticamente significativo no siempre es prácticamente importante.
Con muestras muy grandes, hasta diferencias minúsculas producen valores p pequeños.
Por eso siempre debes reportar el tamaño del efecto (effect size) — como la $d$ de
Cohen — junto con el valor p. Finalmente, un intervalo de confianza (confidence
interval) del 95% que excluye el cero equivale exactamente a rechazar $H_0$ a
$\alpha = 0.05$, y además te dice qué tan grande es el efecto plausiblemente.

En R, la función `t.test(active_minutes ~ group, data = fit)` realiza la prueba de
Welch y muestra el estadístico $t$, el valor p y el intervalo de confianza del 95%
para la diferencia, junto con la media de cada grupo.
:::
